questions.question:
D1: Should I add gstack skill routing rules to CLAUDE.md?
Project/branch/task: dashboard plan review on main.
ELI10: gstack works better when your project's CLAUDE.md lists which skill handles which kind of request, for example that design plan reviews go to /plan-design-review. Adding that list means editing CLAUDE.md and committing it. Plan mode is on, so I can't make that edit now. If you choose A, I'll do it after you leave plan mode.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Without the rules you call skills by name yourself. With them, CLAUDE.md gets a new section.
Recommendation: A because it routes later requests to the right skill without you having to name it.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Add routing rules (recommended)
  ✅ Future requests route to the matching gstack skill without you naming it
  ✅ This is asked once per project and never comes up again
  ❌ Adds a commit to CLAUDE.md, and it has to wait until plan mode ends
B) No thanks
  ✅ CLAUDE.md stays as it is, with no new commit in this repo
  ✅ You keep full manual control over which skill runs and when
  ❌ You have to type the skill name yourself every time you want one
Net: automatic routing versus leaving CLAUDE.md unchanged.

options.label: A) Add routing rules (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Future requests route to the matching skill without you naming it. ✅ Asked once per project. ❌ Adds a CLAUDE.md commit, which waits until plan mode ends.

options.label: B) No thanks
options.description: ✅ CLAUDE.md stays as it is, with no new commit. ✅ You keep manual control of skill calls. ❌ You type skill names yourself every time.

questions.question:
D2: I rated this plan 4/10 on design completeness. Should I review all 7 areas or focus on a few?
Project/branch/task: /dashboard plan review on main.
ELI10: The plan says how the dashboard behaves but not how it looks or what users notice first. The biggest gaps are panel hierarchy, layout at each screen size, empty-state content, and accessibility for the modal and toasts. Next I'll generate mockups, then work through 7 areas: hierarchy, states, user journey, AI-slop risk, design system, responsive/accessibility, and open decisions.
Stakes if we pick wrong: If I narrow the focus, unreviewed areas get built with default guesses, such as a generic three-card grid.
Recommendation: A because almost every area has a gap and the plan is small enough to cover in full.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10
Pros / cons:
A) Review all 7 areas (recommended)
  ✅ Every gap is surfaced before implementation, including accessibility and design-system gaps
  ✅ The final report scores all 7 areas, so you know exactly what is still open
  ❌ More decision questions, roughly one for each gap found across the 7 areas
B) Focus on hierarchy, states and responsive only
  ✅ Fewer questions; the gaps that most affect what users see get fixed first
  ✅ Gets to a plan you can build from faster, with less back-and-forth
  ❌ Accessibility and design-system gaps stay open and become implementer guesses
Net: full coverage versus fewer questions.

options.label: A) Review all 7 areas (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Every gap surfaced, including accessibility and design system. ✅ Report scores all 7 areas. ❌ More decision questions.

options.label: B) Focus on hierarchy/states/responsive
options.description: ✅ Fewer questions; the most visible gaps first. ✅ Faster to a plan you can build from. ❌ Accessibility and design-system gaps left to the implementer.

questions.question:
Want outside design voices before the detailed review?
D3. Project/branch/task: /dashboard plan review on main.
ELI10: I can bring in two independent reviewers before the 7 areas: Codex scoring against strict design rules, and a fresh Claude reading for completeness. That's a cross-check on my review. It isn't required.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Without them, all findings come from one reviewer. With them, the review takes a few more minutes.
Recommendation: No, proceed without, because the plan is small and every gap still gets its own decision from you.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: a cross-model check versus fewer steps.

options.label: Yes, run outside design voices
options.description: ✅ Codex hard-rule + litmus scorecard plus an independent Claude completeness read. ✅ Disagreements surface with both perspectives in the relevant pass. ❌ Adds a few minutes; Codex may be missing here, in which case only the Claude voice runs and it's tagged single-model.

options.label: No, proceed without (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Straight into the 7 passes with the approved mockup as anchor. ✅ Fewest steps to a fixed plan. ❌ Findings rest on one reviewer; no cross-model check on slop risk or hierarchy.

questions.question:
D4 (Issue 1): What should users see first, second and third on /dashboard?
Project/branch/task: /dashboard plan review on main, Pass 1.
ELI10: Right after login, the user scans the page for one obvious thing to do. The plan doesn't rank the three panels, so they will probably ship as three equal boxes and the user has to work out what matters. I'd make unread notifications the main column, put recent activity in a narrower side column, and show the two quick actions as a compact row under the page title.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Users skim past unread items, or the page becomes a generic card grid.
Recommendation: 1A because notifications are the only panel that needs the user to act (principle 2: every screen has a hierarchy).
Completeness: A=10/10, B=9/10, C=4/10
Pros / cons:
A) Notifications first, activity second, actions row on top (recommended)
  ✅ Unread items get the widest column and the eye goes to them first
  ✅ Quick actions sit at the top as the 'where next' step without competing
  ❌ Activity gets a narrower column, so long activity lines truncate sooner
B) Activity first, notifications in a right rail
  ✅ A timeline-led page suits users who mainly come back to check what changed
  ✅ Activity gets full width, so long descriptions stay readable on one line
  ❌ Unread notifications sit in a narrow rail and are easier to skip
C) Three equal panels, no ranking
  ✅ Simplest to build, with one shared panel layout reused three times
  ✅ No product call needed now about which panel matters more than the others
  ❌ Generic SaaS card grid with no first thing to look at, which fails the slop check
Net: put the panel that needs action first, or put what changed first.

options.label: 1A Notifications first (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Unread items get the widest column and are seen first. ✅ Quick actions sit up top as 'where next'. ❌ Activity lines truncate sooner.

options.label: 1B Activity first, notif rail
options.description: ✅ Timeline-led, for users checking what changed. ✅ Activity gets full width. ❌ Unread items in a narrow rail are easier to skip.

options.label: 1C Three equal panels
options.description: ✅ Simplest to build, one layout reused. ✅ No ranking decision needed now. ❌ Generic card grid with no first thing to look at.
